job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, these are potential gaps and drafting problems—not conclusions that a court would invalidate the bill or that every described activity would escape it. Some apparent loopholes could be closed through the discretionary definition in section 2(1)(B), but that provision has its own uncertainties.

### Scope and definitions

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel threshold permits fleet splitting.** The threshold applies to recovery “by a single vessel,” with no aggregation across vessels, operators, or affiliated companies. A company could spread substantial recovery across vessels that each remain below the threshold, unless section 2(1)(B) is invoked.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exactly 10,000 metric tons is outside the automatic definition.** The text covers “more than” 10,000 metric tons, not 10,000 or more. Recovery at or below that amount is not automatically prohibited, even if conducted for commercial sale.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Per year” is undefined.** The bill does not specify a calendar year, a rolling 12-month period, or another accounting period. It also does not explain whether crossing the threshold makes earlier recovery unlawful, complicating compliance and penalty calculations.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement are unclear.** Mining at exactly 200 meters or shallower falls outside the automatic definition, and the text does not specify the reference point or method for measuring depth. Operations spanning different depths could generate disputes about which recovered material counts.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Recovered tonnage lacks measurement rules.** The bill does not distinguish wet weight, dry weight, contained minerals, or material mixed with sediment. Different accounting methods could materially change whether an operation crosses the threshold.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” and vessel attribution are undefined.** The text does not clearly address collection by autonomous equipment, fixed installations, or coordinated collection and transport vessels. Operators could dispute whether recovery occurred “by a single vessel” or whether particular preparatory and processing activities count.

7. **Sections 2(1) and 3(a)—Supporting activities are not expressly prohibited.** Financing, supplying equipment, processing recovered minerals, and purchasing or importing them are not independently banned. Some conduct might constitute participation in prohibited mining, but the bill leaves that boundary uncertain.

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—The responsible “Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines which Secretary makes comparable-risk determinations. Assigning duties separately to NOAA and the Secretary of State does not resolve who holds this central authority.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—The alternative definition lacks substantive standards.** “Risks … comparable” does not specify probability, severity, duration, geographic scale, or a reference mining operation. That uncertainty could support challenges to particular determinations, especially when they underpin criminal liability, although broad agency discretion is not automatically invalid.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—Determination procedures and timing are missing.** The bill does not say whether determinations require rulemaking, individual orders, notice, or an opportunity to contest them. It also leaves unclear when a determination makes an activity prohibited and how operators receive fair notice.

11. **Section 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require a commercial purpose.** The operative definition turns on volume or ecological risk, rather than sale or profit. It could cover noncommercial research while leaving smaller profit-making operations outside the automatic definition, creating a mismatch between the label and actual coverage.

12. **Section 2(2)—“U.S. person” omits numerous entity types.** The definition names citizens and state-organized corporations but does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, permanent residents, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions matter particularly for operations outside the United States.

13. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not covered by ownership alone.** A separately incorporated foreign subsidiary is not a “U.S. person” merely because a U.S. company owns or controls it. The parent’s own participation could still create liability, but the bill has no express ownership, control, or anti-evasion rule.

14. **Section 3(a)—“In the United States” has uncertain geographic reach.** The text does not specify territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. These distinctions matter for foreign operators and entities omitted from the “U.S. person” definition.

### Exceptions

15. **Section 3(b)—Existing exploration licenses receive an open-ended exemption.** The exception has no expiration date, production cap, or environmental conditions of its own. It could preserve substantial mining if that mining is legally conducted under a qualifying exploration license; the exemption does not itself expand what the license authorizes.

16. **Section 3(b)—The qualifying license issuer is unspecified.** The text does not limit the exception to licenses issued by a named U.S. agency or under a particular statute. Operators could argue that foreign or international exploration licenses qualify as well.

17. **Section 3(b)—Transfers, renewals, and modifications are unaddressed.** The bill does not clarify whether grandfathering follows a license after transfer, renewal, expansion, or changes in ownership. This creates uncertainty about whether acquiring or modifying an existing license preserves the exemption.

18. **Section 3(c)—Environmental assessment is an uncapped exception.** The bill specifies no limits on tonnage, duration, location, or equipment used for assessment activities. Large-scale recovery could be claimed as necessary to evaluate environmental effects.

19. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose operations and verification are unaddressed.** The exception does not require assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, prohibit sale of recovered minerals, or require advance approval or independent review. An operator could claim an assessment purpose for an otherwise commercial operation, leaving enforcement to disputed factual judgments.

### Registry and enforcement

20. **Sections 2(3) and 4—The registry misses smaller vessels and non-vessel operations.** Only vessels exceeding 5,000 gross tons and equipped for mineral recovery must register. Smaller vessels can still conduct prohibited mining, so the reporting system does not cover all activities subject to section 3.

21. **Section 4(a)—Registration jurisdiction and deadlines are unspecified.** “Each covered vessel” has no express geographic, flag, or operator-nationality limitation, potentially suggesting an impractically global obligation. There is also no deadline or requirement to register before recovery begins.

22. **Section 4(b)—Reports lack essential specifications and verification.** Operators need only submit certified descriptions of recovery activities; required tonnage, coordinates, depths, measurement methods, records, and submission deadlines are unstated. The bill supplies no express audit or independent verification mechanism.

23. **Sections 4 and 5—Registry violations have no express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other laws might reach some false statements, but this bill provides no specific sanction for simply ignoring the registry requirements.

24. **Section 5—Enforcement authority and procedures are missing.** The bill does not identify a civil enforcement agency or establish assessment, hearing, collection, inspection, subpoena, or seizure procedures. Existing governmental authority may supply some mechanisms, but the text leaves substantial implementation questions unresolved.

25. **Section 5—There is no express injunction or restoration remedy.** Monetary penalties and imprisonment are provided, but the bill does not expressly authorize orders stopping operations or requiring environmental remediation. Other legal authorities might offer relief, but those remedies are not supplied here.

26. **Section 5(a)—Daily penalties are difficult to reconcile with an annual threshold.** The bill does not explain which days constitute violations when recovery becomes “commercial” only after an annual volume threshold is exceeded. This could produce disputes over liability for earlier days, later recovery days, or periods without active recovery.

27. **Section 5(b)—Willfulness and discretionary coverage create notice issues.** Prosecutors must prove a willful violation, potentially making cases harder where operators dispute threshold calculations, exemption eligibility, or a comparable-risk determination. The text does not clarify the required knowledge, leaving courts to interpret the criminal standard.

28. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Penalty dates conflict with delayed effectiveness.** Civil penalties are stated to apply to violations occurring on or after enactment, but the Act takes effect only 180 days later. Because section 3 is not yet operative during that interval, the text creates avoidable uncertainty rather than a clear basis for penalizing interim conduct.

### International coverage and duration

29. **Section 6—Negotiation does not ensure equivalent foreign prohibitions.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate” an agreement, not secure one, and the bill creates no fallback if negotiations fail. Foreign operators outside section 3’s jurisdiction can therefore continue, subject to other applicable law.

30. **Section 7(a)—The condition for lifting the prohibition is underspecified.** “Without serious harm” does not identify the relevant harms, acceptable risk, or whether the finding must apply to all commercial mining or particular methods and locations. A finding concerning a limited technique could prompt disputes over whether the entire prohibition ends.

31. **Section 7(a)—The National Academies report has no commissioning mechanism.** No provision directs anyone to obtain the report, establishes its scope, funds it, or sets a deadline. The purported evidence-based process for ending the prohibition therefore lacks an implementation pathway.

32. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b)—The sunset bypasses the scientific condition.** The entire Act expires after 10 years even if Congress has not found that mining can occur without serious harm. Section 7(a)’s “until” language could suggest otherwise, but section 7(b) supplies an unconditional endpoint.

33. **Section 7(b)—Post-sunset enforcement is not addressed expressly.** The bill does not specify the treatment of pending proceedings, reporting duties, or outstanding obligations after expiration. Federal savings law may preserve incurred penalties, so expiration should not be described as automatically erasing liability.

34. **Section 8—The delayed effective date leaves an interim operating window.** The prohibition does not take effect for 180 days after enactment, permitting continued activity under this bill during that period. Existing legal restrictions would still apply, and licenses issued during the delay would not qualify for section 3(b)’s pre-enactment exception.

**Editorial caveat:** Falling outside this bill’s prohibition would not necessarily make mining lawful under other U.S. laws, foreign laws, or applicable international rules.
